utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have a brief summary and a few questions I'd like to put to the witness. The witness is a survivor of the mass execution near Petkovci of approximately 1.000 Muslim men and boys on the 14th and the early-morning hours of the 15th of July, 1995. On 11 July 1995, the civilian authorities directed that women and children were to go to the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari, whereas the men were to go towards Susnjari. Like thousands of other Muslim men, the witness went to Susnjari where a large column of men and boys between ages 16 and 60 formed and then moved out towards Muslim-held territory. On the night of 12 July, the witness together with about 30 other men were cut off from the main column. The following morning, on 13 July, they encountered heavy shelling. Between Konjevic Polje and Bratunac, the witness could hear Serb forces demanding their surrender over a megaphone, assuring the Muslim men that they would be treated according to the Geneva Conventions and exchanged. The witness and the men in his group decided to surrender. Upon doing so, they carried their wounded along the asphalt road to Konjevic Polje. Along that road, they encountered some 300 other Muslim prisoners who had already surrendered. The men were taken to a hangar near Konjevic Polje where they were detained. Shortly afterward the witness -- shortly after the witness arrived, the prisoners were ordered onto several trucks which then proceeded towards Nova Kasaba. The truck stopped at a sports field where the prisoners were ordered off. They were told to leave their belongings outside before entering. Approximately 15 to 20 Serb soldiers guarded the entrance gates, training their guns on the prisoners and swearing at them. Inside, the witness's group added a new row to the 2500 to 3500 prisoners that the witness estimates were already there when he arrived. About 15 minutes later, General Mladic arrived and addressed the prisoners, after which they were ordered back onto trucks waiting on the road. As the prisoners moved towards the trucks, the witness overheard one prisoner ask a Serb soldier if they should retrieve their bags to which the soldier replied, "You won't need that any longer." Once the witness's truck was filled with approximately 119 prisoners it travelled towards Bratunac, stopping near a supermarket in the village of Kravica. The witness could see at least two other trucks behind his. As it became dark, the soldiers guarding the trucks became abusive toward the prisoners, among other things, striking them with their rifle-butts. At one point the witness saw a soldier put a gun barrel into a prisoners's mouth and threaten, "I will kill you and ten other people if I hear another word being uttered in the truck." The guards called out for prisoners from Srebrenica, Glogova, and other villages. Those who responded were taken out and never returned. Throughout the night the witness heard screams, moaning, cries for help, and bursts of gun-fire. The witness recalled that at approximately 1400 to 1500 hours on 14th July, the prisoners were driven on a truck, escorted by two armed Serb soldiers, in the direction of Zvornik to a school near an aluminium factory in Karakaj. When they arrived, the prisoners were offloaded and told to put their hands behind their heads. They were ordered into the school and forced to chant phrases such as "Long live the Serb Republic" and "Srebrenica is Serb," as they passed between two columns of approximately 20 Serb soldiers that were securing the area. Once inside the witness was taken into a classroom on the second floor where he saw two men who had been beaten and bloodied. The witness recognised one of them. When the classroom was filled with approximately 200 prisoners, Serb soldiers came in and threatened the prisoners, demanding that they turn over their valuables or else be killed. Prisoners were periodically removed from the classroom and the witness could hear gun-fire outside. The witness eventually passed out, and when he awoke only about 15 to 20 prisoners remained in the classroom. Two soldiers soon entered and ordered the witness and three other prisoners out of the courtroom. In the hallway outside the classroom, the witness, along with the other prisoners, was ordered to strip to the waist while his hands were bound. They were then placed in another classroom. About 15 minutes later the witness and several other prisoners were removed and made to board a truck. Once the truck was full, it drove for about 10 to 15 minutes, and when it stopped, the witness could hear gun-fire and yelling. He saw a large lighted field covered with the bodies of prisoners. The witness was ordered off the truck and together with five to ten prisoners told to form a row. They were then taken along a rocky path to the execution site. One soldier ordered the prisoners to lie down. And as they started to comply, the soldiers fired at the prisoners' backs and heads from close range. The witness fell forward over the bodies of prisoners who were already dead around him. Realising that he had not yet been seriously wounded, the witness took cover among the dead bodies. He could hear single shots ring out as the soldiers fired into the heads of wounded prisoners. Another survivor crawled close to the witness and the witness managed to free the prisoner's hands. Together they made their escape, climbing over a mass of dead bodies and then into a wooded area. There the witness saw a large concrete canal where the two eventually hid until first light. The witness heard firing and the sound of heavy machinery coming from the field he had just fled. Just after dawn, as the two survivors attempted to make their escape, they came across a small guard house with a large bulldozer parked in front. They returned to the canal and tried to escape in a different direction. This time they came across a Tarmac road running along a dam, which they crossed. From there, the witness could see bodies being repeatedly loaded onto a large tractor. That evening the survivors started moving towards Tuzla, and they reached the free territory on 18 July 1995. That concludes my summary, Mr. President, and I have a few additional questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, in your previous testimony at page 2.943, lines 3 through 6, you were asked at the time if at the time of the fall of Srebrenica enclave in July 1995, you were a member of the Bosnian army. Your answer was "no." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, following your injury and release from the Territorial Defence in 1992, were you ever mobilised?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. I was mobilised again on the 5th of July. When the attack against Srebrenica started, we were all mobilised in order to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what was your assignment, having been mobilised?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Our assignment was to collect the population, to provide security, to help the -- with the digging trenches, and helping people who were subject to shelling, to help them find their way to the shelters, the women and the children. We did not have any weapons. I didn't have any weapons. Before the Srebrenica fell, I did not have either any weapons or a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that clarification. I'd like to ask you some questions about your time at the football stadium in Nova Kasaba. First could you tell us, how were the prisoners arranged at the time that you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: My group and myself, when we got off the lorry at the very entrance, at the gate, we had to leave all of our things, bags, and everything that had not been taken before at the place where we were first taken prisoners. And then from the gate where we had been awaited by 15 to 20 Serbian soldiers, they started yelling and swearing, and they started distributing us. And I could see that the courtyard was almost full, and my group from that lorry was almost at the very end. We were still filling up that stadium, that courtyard. And according to my estimate, I could see at least 2.000 people there. They were all sitting down. Their hands were on the ground. They were sitting on the grass. And we just followed those who were before us, and then some people came after us. And that's how we went on to fill up that area. And the Serb soldiers were distributed across the entire surface of the stadium. They tried to keep order among us. They made sure that we were all seated down, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you told exactly where to sit or did you just sit where you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, we could not sit where we wanted. As the groups were getting off the truck, they escorted us and made sure that our rows are really tight and that we sat next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I'd like to show you some photographs, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 01101 in e-court, please. All right, if we could -- well, if we could just blow up the right side of the photograph a little bit. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what you see there, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: It's the stadium, the one that I've just described, near Nova Kasaba, where we were taken prisoners. I can maybe point to everything that I've described. If you give me a pen, I can point to the things that I've just described for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have the witness mark the photo, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, if you could indicate for us where it is that you entered, if you can recall --

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The lorries came from Konjevic Polje down this road. This is where we stopped. Do you want me to mark things for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please. If you want to mark the lorries, you can mark it --

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: This road leading towards Konjevic Polje, we can't see it. I can't show you where they came from, but I can show you the general direction. This is where the lorries came from and this is the gate where they stopped. And on the right-hand side the soldiers were standing -- actually, from both sides of the gate, on the right-hand side, and that's where we left all of our bags, next to the gate. And as we entered through the gate, they took us towards the football-pitch, and the football-pitch was already full, everything was full. The people were already sitting there. All the prisoners were already sitting there. Everything was full, which means that when we were escorted inside we were brought to sit here, in the next row, approximately here. As you're looking from Konjevic Polje, we were towards the very end of the football-pitch, somewhere around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if we can mark these with some letters, that might be more helpful. Where the gate is, could you put a letter G, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where the soldiers were, could you put -- that is, the soldiers outside the gates, could you put a letter S where the soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you could, could you put a letter T where the trucks were.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: The trucks came from this direction and they double-parked in front of the gate. I don't know whether they stayed on or whether they proceeded. I don't remember. In any case, before the gate we got off our lorry and that's where the lorry double-parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I take it the X's that you've marked on there indicate the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how they were lined up in rows?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And could you indicate where you were --

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- by putting the letter Y.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Approximately here, where I put my last cross, that's where I was so I'm going to put my Y there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, I would offer this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This photograph with markings will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit IC32. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could have in e-court, please, 65 ter 01166.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another photograph, which I'd like you to identify for us. Witness, do you recognise the picture that's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise them well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: This is the school where we were brought on that evening, from Kravica, where they brought us on the trucks to be executed. I can explain if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If you could explain, that would be helpful. Do you need the pen to explain it, or can you explain it and then we'll mark it?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes -- well, a pen would be fine. But this pen marks so it may not be necessary for me to mark. I remember well that we were brought on trucks and in front of the school we got off. There is also a sports pitch, but it can't be seen here. We had to run in front of the rows of Serb soldiers. I remember well these four or five stairs. The school pitch is at a lower elevation than the school itself, hence the stairs. I remember this double door. It's -- the school is old, and -- yes, I remember this well, I mean this door here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does this photograph depict the entry point that you came in from?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you could, could you just mark where you entered? I think I see a small mark on the doors, but maybe you could make it a little bit bigger so that we could see it.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I can mark. So you go down these stairs and you enter through this door. This is where we entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm going to show you another photograph, if I may, that's 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am going to tender this one. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll wait for the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit IC33. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. If I could show the witness 65 ter 1163, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this picture, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I recognise it. I can see the road on which we were taken to the school, and I can see the sports ground in front of the school. The school where we were tied up in the evening, and in the morning we were taken away for execution. Should I mark anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Just mark the school with an S.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the pitch that you said you ran across, can you mark that? If you can indicate with an arrow.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. Sure, I can do that. The trucks were parked here, in this part of the pitch. Well, the arrow is in the wrong -- points in the wrong direction. Here it is. So we got off the trucks, our hands behind our necks, and there were rows of Serb soldiers. We went down the stairs and entered the school. The entrance is on the right side of this -- well, from this perspective it's on the right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to offer this into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit IC34. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may show the witness, please, 65 ter 1450. I understand it's page 166 in ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it well. This is the school to which we were brought in the evening and from which we were taken away for execution. The stairs that I mentioned in my statement that go down from the first floor, and I was in classroom number 3. I can mark it if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could, that would be very helpful. Are you able to see the classroom you were in from here or the entrance to it?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you to mark that then, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean? Here, now, or when we were -- when we were taken in or out or -- I don't understand. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you able to see the entrance to the classroom where you were held on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: This photograph -- well, I'm not sure I can mark it here. The classroom that we can see I think is number 1, and next to it there is number 2, so number 3 could be somewhere down in this direction so it can't be seen well in this photograph. But I can try to mark it, although you can't really see the entrance well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, if you could mark the direction of the classroom, that would be fine. In other words, if you could point an arrow in the direction you think it might be.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Sure, sure, yeah, I can do that. So we went up to the first floor, we took these stairs, and we went up these five, six stairs; and then there's this platform between the two storeys. I remember this very well. And then you take the next flight of stairs leftward, and the first door I can see here I believe is the entrance to classroom 1. And this iron railing that I mentioned in the statement was the one to which we were tied later on. And this one could be classroom 2, and classroom 3 would be further down this way. So it -- you go down this hallway in this direction and then you'll get to classroom 3, where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And when you were taken out of the building, did you proceed in the opposite direction?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. From the classroom, where there were at least 200 people, as I said, and they took us out four by four. And the group of soldiers, four, five, or six of them, I don't remember exactly, were standing here. And they had ropes and there was a heap of clothes. We had to take all our clothes off to -- and be naked from the waist upwards. And they tied our hands here. They were standing here in the hallway. And once we were tied and undressed, I was pushed into this classroom, number 2. I can't see that the is door open here in this picture, but it was there. And that classroom was packed with people at the time. They were standing close to each other or sitting. There was no light. And I entered this classroom too. Later when they received orders to take us away, they took us through the hallway, where I saw dead people and bloody people. They took us out and we had to get on the trucks that were waiting in front of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just so the record is clear, the classroom 2 that you referred to is the second X from the left of this photograph; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If you could, just put a 2 on top of that.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. Just to make myself clear, once you climb the stairs you go left and the classroom was on the right. So if when we were going down this hallway, the classrooms were all to our right, classroom 2, 3, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could, just mark on the photograph here where you've indicated 1, classroom 1, classroom 2, by writing 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. 1, 2 would be hereabouts, and 3 would be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to offer this one into evidence as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit IC35. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to show you two other photos, if I may. The first is 65 ter 1177. You won't need to mark this photograph, but I would like you to tell us if you recognise what it shows.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: It's a bit blurred, but I think that this is the road that we took behind the school toward the dam. But the photograph isn't very crisp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you another photograph, it's 65 ter 1175. Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it well. I remember it very well. It was the very place where we were executed. I remember this heap of rocks and the canal where we found shelter, and I remember the building up there and a guard house. And there were also lights, reflectors, that were lighted. This is the part below the dam where we were executed in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to offer this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P112. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I could show the witness, please, 65 ter 1174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave the picture on the screen, please, the last one. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just now in your evidence you have stated that this is the site where you were executed; right? Can you indicate the place --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: -- the execution site?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Only the exact location is not visible here in this picture. It shows -- it rather shows the canal where we hid. Perhaps you have another photograph which shows the exact spot. It's further to the right, and we went down this grass and these low shrubs next to these rocks. It was before dawn that we went down to this canal, and I remember these rocks. So we lay in this part. Perhaps there is another photograph that would show the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I misspoke before. What I would like to show the witness is 65 ter 1178, not 1174.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Will that show what the witness wants to show us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could move the photograph a little bit to the left, blow it up and move it to the left, please. That's a little too big. I'm trying to see the right side of the photograph, if we could. Yeah, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise what's depicted in this photograph, Witness?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it well. This is the very spot where we were executed in the evening. The circled and marked area is the spot where we were shot, and we came from the direction of the school and the trucks took us to this spot. And I think I was hereabouts, if I may mark, where I lay. I think it's somewhere here. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see the spot where you lay and where the execution occurred?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. You can see the plateau here, and I can show where I lay, hereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That would be very helpful if you could mark that, please.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. It -- this shows my position roughly, and if I may mark with X's, there were dead people lying everywhere. I don't know how many rows there were, but the field was full. That's what I was able to see. It was lit. There were two large reflectors, so it was all very well lit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please encircle that cross which indicates your position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish all of us peace and may God give that this trial be ended fairly. I don't know why the witness is allowed to show spaces before he -- he is shown a marked photograph. I would kindly ask you to show him in future only unmarked photographs, such that don't contain any markings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As Mr. Tolimir is aware, this is a photograph that was shown to the witness in the course of his previous testimony. This is the photograph that was admitted in relation to that testimony, not through this witness, but in relation to that testimony and was shown to him and it was marked. So I don't see that there is any -- that there is any merit to the objection that Mr. Tolimir has raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you tell us who marked this photo previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My understanding is that the witness marked this photograph previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you indicate the direction of the guard-house, if you can, from this photograph?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I can indicate it. It can't be seen here. Looking from where we were shot, we pulled out to the right, where there was the canal. And the guard-house was behind the dam in this part, hereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could draw an arrow indicating the direction that it would be.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to have this marked photograph admitted, please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit IC36. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has an additional question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Just another question to the witness. While we are on this photograph, can you mark where the canal is for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The canal, yes. The canal was in this direction. You can't see it on this photograph. And here there was a grove and there were -- was undergrowth and grass, and the canal was in this direction, as indicated by the arrow. And we hid in that canal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think that should be admitted as well. Are you tendering that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. President. Thank you. I'd like to show the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We need the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit IC37. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd just like to show the witness again this photograph but from a zoomed-out perspective, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, during the course of your prior testimony you indicated that you were able to see bulldozers or a loader, I should say, and some bodies. Can you indicate -- can you see where on this photograph that occurred; and if you could, can you mark it.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I can indicate it. As we see, the bodies were where I have just showed them to be, and when we crawled out, we went to the canal. We were unable to see anything, but we heard the noise the machines made. And once we started running, we saw from this direction headlights and a strong noise, some kind of tractor or excavator or something, from the direction where we were shot. And we went down to this canal. For a couple of hours we were unable to see anything. When it dawned, we tried to get out of the canal, and then we went in the direction of the guard-house. From there we were able to see the dead bodies and the machinery. We had to go back down to the canal. We went up the road on which we were taken on the previous evening and came across a creek on this side, where we saw a burnt Muslim village and some 300 or 400 metres away we saw these burnt houses. Only the outer walls were standing. We went there to take refuge and hide and perhaps find some food. This is higher up, maybe at an altitude of about 200 metres. And we saw dead bodies lying there, in the field, and we saw the machinery, that is, the loader and the tractor and this backhoe. With the backhoe they were loading the bodies on a truck. But the tractor was taken away in about 15 or 20 minutes. Now, how many people there were exactly, we were unable to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you would, just mark on this photograph where you saw the bodies with X's and where you saw the tractor or the loader with a T.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: The crosses mark where people were lying in the field. The field was completely full. There was a tractor there and there was also the backhoe excavator. Do you want me to mark both the backhoe excavator and the tractor maybe using the same letter? I apologise, because I used X's to mark the dead bodies, and when it comes to the machinery what letters do you want me to use to mark those?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can use the letter T for "tractor" or whatever letter you want, just as long as we've got some indication. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, well, the tractor was around here somewhere, the very beginning of that. And loader excavator started loading the bodies immediately in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the record, the tractor's indicated by T and the loader is marked with a letter U, it appears to be. And I would offer this into evidence as well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit IC38. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to ask you about a few people. I'll ask you their names, and if you would don't indicate any relation you might have with them or relationship you might have with them, but just let me know if you recognise the name. Do you recognise the name Salih Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when was the last time you saw Mr. Mehmedovic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was in the school, in the classroom. We were prisoners together. He had not been feeling well. He asked for water many times. When he tried to go through the door he was returned by the Serb soldiers. He wanted water. The windows were closed and the temperature in the classroom was at least 40 degrees. It was very hot, very sultry, and he was going mad. He wanted a drink of water. He tried to get out of the classroom twice. The second time he went into the corridor. I only heard shots. I could hear them shooting in front of the school. He never returned into the classroom, and after that I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know his father's name?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Emin Emirovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And about how old was he when you last saw him?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Well, I would say 20, 25, 28, at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know -- do you recognise the name Munib Ademovic? And just -- you can tell us if you recognise him or not.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when was the last time -- when and where was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I saw him at the very entrance into the classroom of that school where we were taken to. I saw him by the door at the entrance into the school. He was on -- lying down on the floor. He was covered in blood and I could not recognise him as -- when I saw him. He was not moving or anything. He was just lying down. I also fainted, but when I came to, I saw that there were some 15 or 20 people still in the classroom. And then I saw Munib sitting down. He also had come to, he had been beaten black and blue. I asked him what happened, but he couldn't tell me, he just couldn't utter a word. And that's the last I saw of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know his father's name or about how old he was when you last saw him?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: 45 to 50, I would say, around 50. And I believe that his father's name was Huso. I'm not sure. 99 per cent I'm sure that his father's name was Huso.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name Kadrija Becirovic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I know that name very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: About how old was he when -- the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Between 25 and 28 or 30 at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you also see him at the school?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the same classroom. He was next to me. When they called next four of us to come out, to strip to the waist, and our hands to be tied behind our backs, he was in the same group with me and with two other men I didn't know. When they took us to the truck, we were barefoot, we were walking over blood, and he was loaded on to the truck together with me. And when a Serb soldier started hitting us with a rifle-butt and saying that 20 more could be loaded on to that truck, he was forcing us to sit down but we were unable to sit down because we were so tightly squeezed, as sardines in a box. There was a burst of fire opened at our legs, and then Kadrija says, "I am hit." I don't remember anything else. I know that he fell among us in the lorry and that's the last I heard of him or saw him. And in the meantime the Serb soldiers were shouting, "Alija will take you whether you are dead or alive. We will still be able to exchange you."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recognise the names Safet Krlic, Seval Bektic, Secan Gabeljic, Ramo Fejzic, and Nazim Bujic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were these men with you at the school as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I am very familiar with the names. They were with me in the school, together with many others whose names have not been mentioned, but I remember all of them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Safet Krlic, about how old was he at the time you saw him last, if you can approximate?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: About 40, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about Seval Bektic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: 25, 28. He was a younger man.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Secan Gabeljic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: 50 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ramo Fejzic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Fejzic, with a Z, Fejzic is the name. Fejzic. He was perhaps 40 to 45. I don't know exactly, but that would be his approximate age.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Nazim Bujic?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: He was a younger lad, maybe in his early 20s, 20 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, that concludes my direct examination. Thank you very much, Witness. Thank you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you know that now the accused, Mr. Tolimir, has the right to put questions to you during his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to welcome everybody present, God bless you all. Could the witness please be shown the first page of 1D82, which is a statement provided by him to the OTP on the 16th of August, 1995, where under his profession it says a member of the BiH army and previously a humanitarian worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question: Do you see the statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not on the screen yet. If you can see it, Mr. Tolimir, on your screen then it's already on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is, in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I just wanted to be sure we're not broadcasting this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll ensure that this will not happen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We now can see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Can one conclude from your statement that at the moment when you provided the statement, in August 1995, you were a member of the BH army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I joined the army after the fall of Srebrenica. When I came to Tuzla, the authorities wanted us to become engaged in the BiH army again, and I remained a member until the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the answer's yes?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, after the fall of Srebrenica. However, before Srebrenica fell, I was not a member of the BiH army. I was a civilian and I was working for the civilian structures as a humanitarian aid worker from the 16th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I both -- may I both speakers remind there to pause between question and answer because you are using the same language and the interpreters will not catch what you say. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The person who spoke to the witness was an investigator of the OTP, Susan Castro, in August 1995, and the statement of the security organs of the BiH army was provided to the 31st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D81. Now we can see it on the screen. On the left-hand side is the Serbian version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Witness, are you going to agree with me or are you going to state for the transcript that on the 25th of April you provided -- or, rather, in August 1995, did you tell them that you had provided a statement to the military organs of the BiH army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I believe so. I can't remember. That was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: And I don't know how this error occurred, but it says here that we started on the 12th of July, but we started on the 11th, not on the 12th. I don't know how this error occurred. So it was not on the 12th that we started the interview but on the 11th -- actually, when we started walking from my place on the 11th, at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the 25th of April of this year you stated to the OTP, as the OTP has informed us, after the mobilisation you were never a member of the BH army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No. We did not understand each other. They never asked me about that. I did join the BiH army after the fall of Srebrenica enclave. When we reached Tuzla, I joined the BiH army again. They didn't ask me again whether I rejoined the BiH army. I only said that I wasn't a member of the BiH army when Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To the organs of the BH army, when you provided your statement on the 31st of July, 1995, you stated that you are a salesperson by trade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a salesperson. That was my last professional, my last occupation, actually. I did other things as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you provided a statement to the OTP and that you said that from December 1992, you were never a member of the BiH army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: From December 1992? I don't remember December. I said from June 1992 on -- from the 16th of June, when I was wounded, when I was transferred to the humanitarian aid sector, and I worked for the civilian population. But I don't remember ever mentioning December. I don't remember ever mentioning anything about the month of December anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said to the OTP that you were demobilised in 1992 and that after that, you were never a member of the BH army; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't remember. I was demobilised after I was wounded. I was wounded, and then from the military structures I was transferred to the civilian structures on the 16 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "civilian structures"? Did they have any obligations vis-a-vis war activities and the activities that were carried out in keeping with war activities?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Of course, it is all related because we protected the population, the women, the children. We protected the shelters. We were distributing food. We had to provide security for the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which means that you performed duties and activities which had to do with the security of the citizens and population in the territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that be the members of the TO, volunteers, members of the BiH who did that? Who was supposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What was your capacity when you performed the duties that you have just described? Let me not go over the same ground again. What was your capacity? What was your position? Which organs did you belong to or were subordinated to when it came to the performance of your task?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Organs of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and Mr. Tolimir please be asked to: A, slow down; B, make pauses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand now. When it comes to the bodies of civilian protection, would they belong to the scope of the organs that are engaged in the defence jobs?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Not in peace time, but during the war I suppose that they can also be engaged in such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement that you provided to the organs of security on the 31st of July, 1995, which is 1D81, on page 1 you stated the following.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look for the statement in question, 1D81, we have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll start reading, and I quote: "With our families" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down, Mr. Tolimir. You are still much too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the statement I am reading and I quote: "With our families we went to the village of Lehovici and then we parted ways. Able-bodied men started walking towards Jaglici, which is a village. And from Jaglici, the column was moving towards Buljim."

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "When we reached Siljkovici we received an order that we should count ourselves and rest because shells were falling all the time along the road and we came under fire from anti-aircraft machine-guns and anti-aircraft guns. And when we got to the woods in Siljkovici, the order was given for us to head in the evening towards the asphalt road" --

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: -- "that is to say, in the direction of Konjevic Polje."

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As I have just read out, you stated in that statement that you able-bodied men set off towards Jaglici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question to you is this: What do you mean when you say "able-bodied men"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Every man from the age of 14, 15 onwards was considered to be an able-bodied person, an able-bodied man, but we didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. In this statement you also say that orders were given. You said it twice. And you mention the first one to rest and to count heads, and the second was about the time and the direction of your movements. And my question to you, sir, is this: Who was it who issued those orders and who was it who counted you?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know who issued orders. I really don't know anything about that. I only heard, in that column, that we were to wait, and when it came to the counting of heads it was all of us who counted ourselves in the way we knew each other, the way we belonged to local communes, we walked in groups and we counted each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And then would the representatives of each village count heads and report on the head count?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, this could not happen. Nobody was in a position to count so many people; and second of all, we hit a Chetnik ambush and all-out shelling and we lost most of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Can you tell us a bit more about the orders for you to rest, to count heads? What can you tell us because you did not just mention that in passing. We can't just skip that very important bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: As I've already told you, I believe every representative of a village, of a local commune, had made some arrangements to look after the people. We just -- couldn't just walk blindly as cattle. There should have been some order instilled among us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. During your testimony in the Krstic case, on page 2943 you stated, and I quote: "We simply received an order from the civilian structures that all of us had to leave Srebrenica enclave." And then you say, in Susnjari, [indiscernible] men, and the women and children to Potocari. And in your statement that you provided to the OTP, the second paragraph, you say: "I believe that the order came from the command of the Bosnian government in Srebrenica." Is everything that I've just read out true and fair and correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I suppose so. I don't know who it was who issued any orders. When Srebrenica fell and when Chetnik and Serb forces occupied Srebrenica, we had to start moving, we had to go somewhere. I don't know who had issued the order. I don't know. We had to start moving. We had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you stated in the Krstic case that the civilian structures had issued that order, representatives of the civilian authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Srebrenica issued that order?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't remember. If that's what I said, that may have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember that in your statement that you provided, on line 8, statement number 0081-8581, you said the following --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The number that the interpreter has just read is probably not correct because it was read by Mr. Tolimir too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2. Could that please be shown. 1D82. We don't see it yet. Page 2. Page 2 of the statement, please. Page 2. Thank you. Now we can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you count to number 8, line number 8, and in the second sentence you said: "I believe that the order came from the Bosnian authorities in Srebrenica. We went together, men and women, until we reached the village of Lehovici, where we split. "The men continued walking towards Susnjari, and in" -- and we will not go on. Did you state this in your statement? Do you see here what is written?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement that you provided to the OTP, the second paragraph, it says: "I believe that the order came from the Bosnian authorities in Srebrenica." Is that correct? Was that indeed the case?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I totally do not understand you. What are you asking me to tell you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did an order arrive from the representatives of the Muslim government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Srebrenica? You stated that in your statements, on the transcript, in the statements. Is it correct -- previously you stated who it was who issued the order, and now you say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I suppose that there was somebody who issued that order. We could not just start walking. As soon as Srebrenica fell, as soon as Serb forces entered Srebrenica, somebody must have issued a -- an order for the people to leave Srebrenica and to start walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us when it was when you received that order, what day, 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th, 15th, when?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can personally confirm I was there when we were trying to save the population, when it was said that there would be NATO bombing of Serb positions, but nothing came of it. In the evening around 5.00, or 1700 hours, on the 11th of July, in the afternoon, we started leaving our place of residence. It was on the 11th of July, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I stopped you because you are not waiting for the -- the transcript has finished. We need the proper translation and the transcript must be finished, and then you can start with your next question, not earlier, please. And again, my wish to both of you, please slow down by answering and putting questions. It's not possible for the interpreters to follow at this speed. Please carry on but slow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you receive the order on the 11th, before you started moving? It is possible that you started moving once you received the order on the 11th at 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know how the order was issued, who it was who issued the order. News spread. There was a state of panic. Can you imagine a situation when people were being killed, when houses were being torched? The Serb forces were slaughtering people, killing children and women, and destroying everything on the way. Can you imagine the state of panic, the state of terror, and at that moment I don't know who issued the order, how it was issued. News reached us that we were supposed to start moving, and we did that, that very moment. We did not have the time to think. I don't know whether the order came before that or when. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait. And now you carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I understand you, and please don't repeat what you have already said because I need some time. You said clearly that the civilian structures issued it, but now you say you don't know how. And a minute ago you said that the VRS had entered Srebrenica on the 11th. Is that correct? Because so far, you had been saying that they weren't there yet.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I can claim with full responsibility that they entered in the evening hours of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Tolimir seems to be misstating the record, and I just want to -- the question in this particular instance ultimately was okay, but the lead-in to the question substantially misstated the record on this case. The witness testified repeatedly that he does not know who issued the order. And so yet there has been no change in that circumstance since the beginning of this line of examination. I just want -- I just want to alert Mr. Tolimir to that because I will be objecting to that if he continues in this line. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should bear that in mind. I think this is a relevant objection by the Prosecution, but now we have reached the proper time for our first break. And I would like to remind you both again to slow down, especially if you are quoting any statement or other parts of the written documents. We adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, before you continue, we have received before the break several photos with markings as exhibits, and they were assigned IC numbers. This is not the way we have received documents with previous witnesses, and therefore I asked the Registrar to assign different numbers, P numbers, to these exhibits and they will be now read out for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. And I apologise. IC32 shall be assigned Exhibit 113. IC33 shall be assigned Exhibit P114. IC34 shall be assigned Exhibit P115. IC35 shall be assigned Exhibit P116. IC36 shall be assigned Exhibit P117. IC37 shall be assigned Exhibit P118. IC38 shall be assigned Exhibit P119. That will be all, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now, Mr. Tolimir, go ahead with your cross-examination, but please bear in mind to be very slow. It's impossible to have a sufficient record if you continue asking questions with this high speed. It is impossible for the interpreters and the court recorder. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, please answer my questions first and then comment, because otherwise both the point of my question and your answer is lost if you start with a comment or stating reasons. I asked you whether the civilian authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina or Srebrenica said anything, and you are supposed to say yes or no or -- because if you start otherwise, then it will seem that I misquoted or stated something wrong, et cetera. So please answer my question first and then comment if you feel the need to.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: If I said something in a statement, then probably it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a court of law. If you say "probably" to my question, then that means that your statement given in 1995 isn't correct.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, I'm sure that the statement has been correctly translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are in the position to put questions. To give such a guidance is the duty of the Chamber. Please carry on your cross-examination and put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your microphone must be switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, on transcript page 2943 you said: "We went to the Lehovici hill, where we split. All women and children went to Potocari camp and the men toward Susnjari." My question to you is: Was that an order, for you to split at Lehovici, were you split from the women and children or was it your own decision?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody issued an order, but we knew if the men were to go to Potocari that nobody would be saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That's your opinion. You answered my question.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: That was my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I didn't ask for your opinion. I only asked you to confirm whether or not what I read out is true.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, it is true what you have read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness the 65 ter document 01450 on page 5. It's a Prosecution 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said you'd -- so you're saying you don't want to answer? All right. Then you refuse.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: But please refrain from mentioning my place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Then please indicate Lehovici and the village of Siljkovici, mark them 1, 2, and 3 respectively.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I know the territory of Bosna-Herzegovina, and I know where Srebrenica is. I also know where Tuzla is, but it is difficult to indicate the exact position of any particular village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that you are unwilling to mark the positions. Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't want to indicate the positions of those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer me. When you arrived at Susnjari, did you say in the Krstic case that according to the assessment of the municipal authorities, there were some 13.000 to 14.000 people there. Do you remember what you stated in the Krstic trial?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us to what municipal authorities were you referring then?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean, which municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What municipal authorities made the assessment that there were 13.000 to 14.000 people?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: It was based on the census which was carried for -- carried out before the fall of Srebrenica, and in that territory there was a population of 65.000 people, roughly, in that enclave, including men, women, and children. So according to an assessment, the number of men who had set out for Tuzla was about 15.000, but nobody was in a position to count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mention anybody's name who made that assessment of 13.000 to 14.000, as you stated at General Krstic's trial?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I cannot mention any names nor do I know who exactly made that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in the Popovic case, on page 2D44 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 2944.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is actually the Krstic case. "There were about 13.000 to 14.000 people at Susnjari." However, on page 2945, lines 3 to 5, Prosecutor Harmon asked you a question. "I understood that the people in that group of about 15.000 people left the enclave in a column. Is that correct?" Now, here we must clarify whether you are saying is correct 13.000 to 14.000 or what Harmon said, 15.000. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can repeat that the number was somewhere between 13.000 and 15.000 thousand. Nobody could have counted them, nor were they indeed counted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So all these estimates were rough estimates without any counting or without establishing the exact number by using any lists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But which estimate is correct then, because you said 13.000 to 14.000, Harmon says 15.000. What is correct, Harmon's statement or yours?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Well, you tell me how many there were exactly. You are in a position to say also.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You are the witness and the Trial Chamber is eliciting information from you, not from me. You're stating a fact for the transcript, not for me.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I said that the estimate of the number was from 13.000 to 15.000, and that can be found in all structures and in all protocols.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I'm not asking you what you have just said, but whether you stated for the transcript in the Krstic trial that there were 13.000 to 14.000.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact number that I stated, but if it was recorded on paper then that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You went on to say on page 2945 of the transcript, lines 7 and 8: "The column was formed. The order was to go through Serb lines. There were 7.200 kilometres to the free territory, Tuzla." Obviously, here, the distance is wrongly stated because 7.200 kilometres is the distance found in the transcript. Can you now say how long the column exactly was or what you -- what was your statement about it?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Do you mean the length of the column?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I said from 7 to maybe 10 kilometres. It may not have been recorded, but nobody was in a position to measure the length of the column. The column -- a column was formed and we want to pass through Serb lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait to the end of the translation. And now put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you had received an order to pass through Serb lines. So a column was formed to pass through Serb lines. Can you tell us what the order exactly said. How should you pass through Serb lines? Please explain to the Trial Chamber, not to me. I'm asking questions for the Trial Chamber to know.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can only repeat. I don't know how orders were issued and to -- and by who. Imagine a crowd of 15.000 people. How can you have order there? I only know that news were received that we had to go through Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Earlier you were saying 13.000 to 14.000, now you're saying 15.000. You must adhere to your statements. That's my plea to you. Do not confuse us with differing statements.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse anybody, and I don't want to be asked such questions. If I said 13.000 to 15.000, then I stand by that statement. I didn't count them, though, nor could anybody at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you have put this question several times to the witness and you received a sufficient answer. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My -- I'm satisfied with a yes/no answer by the witness. I don't need elaboration. I just want concrete answers to my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what your question was, so I don't know what to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you whether you knew who had issued the order to pass through the Serb columns, just say "I know" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, on page 2944, lines 18 through 24, you were asked about the composition of the column, and the Prosecutor is being recorded as quoting you that the column was made of men aged between 16 and 65, and you also said that there were a few women and younger women who were accompanying their boyfriends. There were 200 to 300 women. Is this an error in the transcript or is it indeed what you stated?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you sure that there were 200 to 300 women?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I repeat again, there is -- nobody could count heads, nor did it ever occur to anybody to count people in the column. However, judging by the list of missing persons, a conclusion was reached that the figure was between 200 and 300.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please -- could you please wait for the answer. Now put the question or your request.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D1, page 12 and 14 -- in English and 14 in B/C/S. This is Becirovic's statement. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see Becirovic's statement here and he says, and I quote: "There were not many women in the column and I didn't see many children either. There may have been some dozen women." Becirovic was the commander of that column. Thank you. Is that correct or not? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: First of all, let me say that I do -- I cannot read the small print. Second of all, I don't know who Becirovic is, I don't know anything about the statement. I know what I said, what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ten and 11 -- 11th line from the top, you will see he says that there were not many women in the column, and he also says that he didn't see many children either. Thank you. That's line 27 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't want to embark on a discussion as to what that Becirovic stated. I don't know who he is. I adhere by my own words.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask you that. I can only tell you that this statement was provided to the organs of the BiH army and that they recognised Becirovic as the commander of that column, and I suppose that they know who was in command of the column. Can you tell us, please, for the transcript, in his statement does it say what I have just read out, that there were not many women?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you didn't indicate which line you were quoting. I didn't find it in the quoting -- just a moment, please, and you got the answer from the witness that he doesn't know the person who gave this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In the English-language version it is page 14, line 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was this: Does he believe that what he said was correct, about 200 to 300 women, or whether Becirovic was correct, who said that there were not many women, maybe not more than ten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat. I don't know. I don't want to discuss Mr. Becirovic's statement. I don't know the man. I only know and I adhere by my words, by what I stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this answer you have already received before, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the nature of the question itself is inappropriate to put to the witness. It's inappropriate to question the witness about the veracity of another witness's statement or to compare his statement to another witness's statement. It's the nature of the objection. I understand the witness has answered it, but I think Mr. Tolimir would be well advised on that specific legal issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, put questions to this witness what he knows, what is his estimation. That is the most helpful way for your cross-examination. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is precisely what I'm trying in order to understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on. Don't explain and don't discuss it with the Chamber. Please carry on. Put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, when you started moving towards Potocari, as you have just explained - and you said that it was on the 11th around 1700 hours - was the Serbian army already in Potocari when you started moving towards Susnjari? This is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I didn't go to Potocari at all. Women and children went to Potocari. We, as I have already told you, started moving in the direction of Susnjari, or rather, Jaglici. There are actually two or three villages or hamlets bearing different names and all in the direction of Buljim.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Could you please hold on just a moment. I need to provide a bit lengthier explanation. At that moment I don't know whether the Serb forces had entered Potocari, but I claim with full responsibility that they did enter Srebrenica in the evening on the 11th, they entered the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I spoke about that because for a while you were moving towards the village of Lehovici together with the women, and then the women and the men separated. They went to Potocari and you proceeded. I thought that you understood me. If you didn't, let me repeat. Before you were separated from the women and the children, before you started moving towards Susnjari and they started moving towards Potocari --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, don't repeat all your explanations. You are not giving evidence. Please put questions to the witness. You are in cross-examination with this witness. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone. It is not translated and not recorded otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness whether the Serbian forces were in Potocari around 1700 hours, when the families started moving towards Potocari and Susnjari. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
