utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer whether they were there at 1700 hours because I was not in Potocari. I told you that they had entered Srebrenica on that day, in the evening, and you're asking me something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just answer my question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I said what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In your statement you stated that the Serbs had confiscated a UN vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When did you hear that the Serbs had confiscated a UN vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: We heard that between the 10th and the 11th, when the DutchBat had withdrawn from Zeleni Jadar, I don't know what the elevation or the feature number was. I believe that their vehicle was taken already on the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And did the Serbs take that vehicle away or did it remain in position?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: The Serbs took it away for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this statement and in your previous statements you stated that you had received an order for militarily able-bodied men to go to Susnjari and that the women and the children should go to Potocari. The order that was issued by the civilian authorities in Srebrenica, as you stated, did it leave people free will to decide whether they would go to Susnjari or to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt the witness, but I feel that I need to object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I saw you on your feet --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and just wait for -- that you get the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to hear the answer, and then it is up to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course people could choose, but at that moment, very few people, if any at all who were either sick or disabled, went to Potocari. They did not believe that the Serbs would ever get to Potocari, or rather, they didn't want to get into the Serb hands and they feared they would if they went to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And I apologise for interrupting the witness. The question was put, again which I think misstates the evidence in this case, that there was an order that was "issued by the civilian authorities in Srebrenica, as you stated," is how it was put to the witness in this case. This witness has repeatedly said that he does not know who issued the order. He stated that he believes that it was civilian authorities previously, but he's never said in this trial, or any trial, that it was the civilian authorities who issued the order. This is a fact that Mr. Tolimir has repeatedly misstated in putting questions to the witness. The ultimate question was a different one altogether. And so I think otherwise it stands, but I am concerned about this really misstating the evidence in this case. And I want to -- I want Mr. Tolimir to be aware of that. I don't know if it's a translation error or something else, but it's very clear in this case what the witness's answer has been up until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have the answers of the witness on the record. We have previous testimony received in evidence. We have all that and we dealt with this problem already. I think this witness is able to answer the question from his knowledge and we will receive the evidence as it is necessary. But on the other hand, Mr. Tolimir, be very careful quoting in the correct way. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The statement has been given to me by the OTP. It is 1D82. And it clearly shows what the witness stated. Can I please read this just to demonstrate whether he said that or whether he said what Mr. Vanderpuye is now saying? Thank you. It's just one sentence. Thank you. Things are always in dispute here because nothing is elaborated properly and nothing is brought to a proper end. The witness says in the statement that I'm just quoting from on page 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you please indicate exactly where you are quoting from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D82. The witness's statement provided to the International Tribunal, lines 8 and 9, on page 2 of the statement, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment so that we have it on the screen. Line 8 and 10, you said. Is it in English or in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 8 and 9 of the Serbian version, 8 and 9 of the Serbian version because the witness speaks Serbian, and the same applies to the English version, where it says: "I believe that the order arrived from the authorities of the Bosnian government (BiH) ... in Srebrenica." And this is what I quoted, nothing else. I didn't quote anything else. I'm -- and I asked the witness whether it is correct that he stated that, and since I didn't receive an answer at the beginning, all of a sudden it's a problem and Mr. Vanderpuye's objecting to that. I just wanted to hear whether the witness stated that in his statement provided to the International Tribunal, yes or no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not found it yet, but if you are reading from my statement that means that I have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at the statement. It's in front of you. It's in the second paragraph, the second, third, fourth sentence in line 4, second sentence: "I believe that the order came from the command of the Bosnian government in Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Was that your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose I said so, especially if that's how it was recorded. I've told you several times that I don't know who issued those orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Were there any military commanders in the column? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I suppose that there were, but I didn't know them and I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please. Who was in charge of the column, military commanders or civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know who was in charge of the column. I don't know who was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us then or can you confirm that both exerted influence on the column; is that how we are to understand your answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can't claim anything. As I've just told you, 15.000 people or anything between 13.000 and 15.000 people in one place, who was it -- who was there to instill any order to that mass of people?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D47. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just yes or no. Do you recognise the person in this photo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, I don't recognise this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please write the word "unknown" on the photo.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please write that on the photo? It's a document. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not a sufficient way. You have the answer on the record. We have on the record which photo was shown to the witness, and this is enough of evidence. It's not necessary to make any markings of this kind, and we will recommend the Prosecution to do the same. We have everything on the record and it is very clear that he said that he doesn't know. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness then be shown 1D48. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you tender this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to tender this photo, and I would like the next document to be displayed, 1D48. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D47 shall be assigned Exhibit D26. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, could you please identify the face that you see in this photograph? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can identify him, but I don't know why you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A minute ago I asked you whether there were any commanders in the column and you said you didn't know. I now must identify some of these persons, and probably later I will have additional questions. But first say yes or no. You didn't know the first man but you know this one?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I know him somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that person in the column? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I didn't see him personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I stop you here. Witness, you were asked if you know this person and you said you recognise him but you don't know why you were asked by Mr. Tolimir. This is not a proper question of you. You should say you recognise him, do you know who it is, and then tell the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I recognise him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this photograph into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document shall be assigned Exhibit D27. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have 1D50, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, can you identify the persons in this photograph, and if you can, tell us who they are.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, I don't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now see 1D52, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, please tell us if you know who the person is who's reading from the sheet of paper and what was his position.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I cannot recognise the person with the paper. I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we please see 1D82, page 2, paragraph 5 of both the Serbian and English versions. Now let us see the fifth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate what kind of document this is. It seems to be a statement, but of whom and to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the statement of this witness, and I gave the reference, 1D82. This is a statement that he gave to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph, I'm reading the last three lines, quoting: "Fire was opened on different parts of the column. The column had to stop during the shelling. I heard that there were many wounded and killed by the shelling, but I didn't see this." Witness, do you remember the statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I gave this statement, but I doubt that these are my initials. I don't remember ever initialling this way. I stand by everything I said except for the last thing. It reads "I did not see this," but I did see that. On the first occasion we were ambushed, there were people both killed and injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you saw it, then tell us how many were injured or were killed, because here you say, "I didn't see this."

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: 40 to 50 wounded persons were carried from Jaglici to the first ambush at Kamenica in the evening, and maybe a dozen people were killed. I said that but it may not have been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us at which locations were you ambushed and when the column was first shelled in the early-morning hours of the 12th of July, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. The -- I don't know the exact locations, but I can say that as soon as we entered Buljim, which was on the Serb-controlled territory, in the early-morning hours the shelling started and our column was fired at from an anti-aircraft gun when we went from Kravica to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 of your statement, sixth paragraph, you can see it, you say: "We continued to walk until we reached a forest near the village of Siljkovici at around 1530 hours on the 12th of July. The shelling continued off and on all the time. The column had broken up into groups. Everyone was looking for neighbours and friends. I didn't count the people around me. I was separated from my brother and I haven't seen him since. I heard 30 people were killed and left by the river and that 24 (as interpreted) were wounded and taken off to the forest." Have I quoted you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I was following what you read from the statement, but I didn't write it all that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, there was one problem. You quoted that 24 were wounded, but on the statement we saw 42. That was perhaps a misreading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, that it was wrong. The witness said 42 in the statement that the Prosecution forwarded to us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you doubt that what you said is true?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't doubt it. I don't know exactly how this is stated, but I said that the first time we were ambushed, that there were people killed and injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that there were a dozen killed and the others were wounded, 40 to 50, on the first ambush; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And were 30 killed after the second shelling?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Even more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you say how many?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: You are burdening me. I didn't dare raise my head, let alone count the dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So your estimate is more than 30?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility there were over 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. You say that there were over 100. Which river was that where these hundred -- 100 people were killed, near what village was that?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know the area. I'm telling you. I had never been there. There was a small river or brook from Koprivna [phoen], and that brook downstream flowed into the Kravica, but I don't know its name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. On page 3 of this statement, could we please turn to page 3, it is page 3 of the English version as well, third paragraph, you speak about the shelling of the column that followed. And you say: "The shelling killed and wounded many people. When I" -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "I saw approximately 30 to 40 bodies. I don't know what happened to the wounded from the first attack on our column." My question is: Was that the second attack, the second shelling, where you said that about 100 were affected?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. Here it says I don't know what happened to these 30 to 40 people, but I meant the ones that were -- that were killed in the first ambush and they were carried away. But in the evening, we were ambushed for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about the location where you say that over 100 people were killed?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean exactly, tell you anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: A description of the terrain where that river was.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Well, I can only repeat that I had never been there before and it was night. We were in a group. I know approximately where it was, between Buljim and the village where we were captured on the following day when we descended from Sandici. It was to the left of the Kravica, in a forest. I cannot give you the names of the individual locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Can you now tell us who led the column to that place where it was scattered, as you say?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can only repeat that I don't know who led the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this statement you described the column and speak about suicides in the column; is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I said that there may have been some suicides because once that poison was used against us, tear gas, et cetera, well, people may have reacted frantically, but there can't have been many suicides.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I read -- I found in your statement that you say many in the column committed suicide. Can you describe that incident to us, like the two brothers who got in a fight with weapons?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I only heard that they were brothers. I don't know them. I heard that there was such an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that one had an automatic rifle and the other a semi-automatic rifle, and that they used these weapons against each other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Well, if I said as much, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also said that many used hand-grenades against each other, that there was a group of four or five people who held each other by the hands and used hand-grenades, and there was much blood all around. And you say, I quote: "I couldn't look at the bodies any longer. I saw more than 40 bodies at the spot where I was. My relative and I took some water from the river and we continued." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, I didn't state it that way. That I saw 40 bodies on a heap, that's most certainly not what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at page 2 of your statement. I can see that it's the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 4. Can we see that, please. Can we please see page 4 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see it on the screen? We don't have it on our screens yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see it, not the Serbian version. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbian, page 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... ask for page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is page 4.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness kindly look at the last two lines in this paragraph. I quote: "I could not look at the bodies anymore. I saw about 40 bodies total" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness can see it. These are the last two lines of the first paragraph on page 4 of the Serbian version of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote the last two lines: "I could not look at the bodies anymore. I saw about 40 bodies total in the immediate area that I stayed in. My cousin and I took some water from the river and continued." Thank you. Witness, my question is: You gave this statement to the OTP and we got it from them. You now claim -- do you now claim that something was entered in this statement that you never said?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't remember that I said anything about 40 bodies. I saw a number of people, but 40 bodies, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But did I quote correctly? Is that what your statement says?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you give us any details about this location where these suicides were committed? You said that it was by a river. Can you say which river?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can repeat once more that it was a river that we passed on our way from Kamenicko Brdo to the spot where we were taken prisoner on the following day. I don't know the name of that small river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 4 of your statement which we have before us right now, you say in the Serbian version - and the translation is on page 5, first paragraph, and the Serbian version is page 4 - and I quote: "I heard that the Serbs had confiscated APCs from the United Nations at the UNPROFOR check-point as well as in Kiprova and Jadar, and that they had taken them away towards Milici." My question is this: Who did you hear it from, did you hear that in the column, and when did you hear that information?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I didn't hear it in the column. I heard that immediately before the fall of Srebrenica, on the 10th, in the evening, when Zeleni Jadar had fallen and when the Serbs had taken that check-point. I heard that the Serb forces were approaching Srebrenica. I heard news that the UNPROFOR APC had been captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were arrested you arrived at the football-pitch, as you say on page 2D50 [as interpreted], line -- lines 23, 24 of the Krstic transcript. You said that at the football-pitch in Nova Kasaba, according to your estimate, there were about 2.000 to 3.000 people. However, on page 5 of your statement provided to the OTP you said that there were about 2.000 people. Could you please tell us here, before this Trial Chamber, which information is correct. Is it 2.000 or 2.000 to 3.000? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: You keep on repeating your questions all the time. I said 2.000 to 3.000. At that moment nobody could count the people. I just assumed that that was the full capacity of the football-pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I respect any answer. I'm not underestimating any of your answers. You said 2.000 to 3.000. I actually just quoted back to you what you said at different times. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 01450, page 33. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recognise the photo? Was it also shown to you in the Krstic case and has it been shown to you here?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise it and yes it was shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2D52 [as interpreted] in the Krstic case, you said that the football-pitch was packed with Muslims and that at the gate there were 15 to 20 Serb soldiers. You stated that in answering the Prosecutor's question, you said that there were 15 to 20 Serb soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Also in your statement provided to the OTP, page 5, paragraph 4, in the English version, you stated, and I quote: "I was sitting together with the other prisoners for some 20 minutes or so, and then I saw Ratko Mladic getting out of an APC. It was on the 13th of July, between 1400 and 1430 hours." Then after that you stated this: "Mladic was standing on a stage which was erected in the football-pitch." Could you please confirm whether this is correct or is there something that you failed to mention?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: This is a fair representation of the situation. We were there for some 15 to 20 minutes. The stadium was already packed, and then Commander Mladic came and he personally addressed us and asked whether we knew him. I don't know if he was standing on a stage or whether he was standing on a step which was in front of us. I said that I couldn't -- I cannot be sure because I didn't see him. He was standing outside of the football-pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And now as you're looking at the photo, could you please mark the place where you were and could you put number 1 next to that place? Could you also mark the place where Mladic was and put number 2 next to that. And could you please mark the place where the Serb soldiers were standing and put number 3 next to that place. Thank you. First draw a circle and then put numbers to each of the circles.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: As I've already said to the Prosecutor, the place where I was standing was somewhere around here. This is number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: And what else do you want me to mark?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The stage and Mladic is number 2.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I repeat, I don't know whether there was a stage at all or whether there was something else from before. He was standing in front of the -- in front of us. This is where he came and he was standing by the goal-posts, and I can put number 2 next to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: About here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what about the Serb soldiers, where were they?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers were distributed across the entire pitch. They were keeping order across the football-pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please mark that?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I can put some crosses where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: These are the soldiers, number 3, but there were several of them across the entire football-pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You are saying or actually are you saying that there were 2.000 to 3.000 of us? Are you saying that the stadium could accommodate 2.000 to 3.000 people, plus the stands, plus the soldiers, and everything else?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please put a square in the photo to show us where the prisoners were sitting, and leave the room for the stands and for the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I have already done it before, but let me do it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go on, just put a line, a square, a line around the area where the prisoners were. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: How can I draw that? The entire field was packed with people. Can you imagine --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I apologise, but there has to be a stage, there have to be soldiers. Could you please draw a line around the area where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I'm repeating once again, I don't know. I could not even see whether there was a stage or step or some sort of a contraption. In any case, we were all seated and we could see Ratko Mladic standing here with a group of soldiers, the Serb soldiers who were guarding him, and that's the place from which he addressed us, scolded us, and promised us that we would all be exchanged, that we would be given food and water, and finally he killed us all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please draw any kind of line to show the area where the prisoners were.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yeah, I can mark the entire stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Okay. Mark the entire stadium.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Okay. I can mark the entire stadium, then. I apologise. The entire football-pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this photo please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this photograph shall be assigned Exhibit D28. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, on page 2994, a segment of your statement was quoted. I will be reading only the quote. "The Serbs asked who participated in the take-over in Kravica when it fell under the BiH control." In your statement, in the Serbian language, it's the penultimate paragraph on page 5. And your answer to that was this and I quote from that same transcript: "I don't remember and I don't know how this was translated." Could you please explain the source of confusion. Why did you mention the translation here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't hear anybody asking if I knew who had taken over power in Kravica. I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown his own statement, page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you could repeat the number of the document again. There's some confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D82, page 5, penultimate paragraph in the Serbian language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we should make clear that this will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version you will find the same quote on page 5 in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness whether in his statement he stated, and I quote: "The Serbs asked who was it who had taken part in the take-over in Kravica when Kravica fell under the control of BiH." That's page 5, penultimate paragraph. And now the witness says that he doesn't remember that that came up at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it here; however, I don't remember anything about Kravica. I know that they were looking for some people from the villages surrounding Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So I quoted your words correctly. I did not make anything up. I just want to prove that I quoted your words properly. Just please state for the transcript whether I could quote your words properly, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There are quite a few discrepancies between your statement provided to the security organs and the OTP. I don't know why that is, but just for the transcript I would like to repeat that on the 31st of July, 1995, you provided a statement to the security organs of the BiH army. And then in August 1995 you provided a statement to the OTP. So we are talking about a time difference between July and August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have all that on the transcript. It's not necessary to repeat it again. Just put questions to the witness. We are in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, were you able to read the statements in both cases, in the case of the statement provided to the security organs as well as to the OTP, before signing them?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you sign them?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This part of the transcript will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. If he keeps on revealing my identity, I will ask you to stop the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will not reveal your identity. Thank you for the warning. There are people here who control the transcript and the broadcast, and you can behave any way you want. Thank you. Could you please tell us what do you mean when you say "the collection of humanitarian aid"? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: That concerned the collection of food for the refugees. We had a lot of refugees from other municipalities, and we had to look after their dietary needs and their accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that the reason why there are different versions about your profession? In the BiH army statement you said that you were a sales assistant, and then you said to the OTP that you were a humanitarian aid worker. Is that only because you wanted to explain your role or were you really engaged in all those different professions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: When I mentioned my occupation or profession, I suppose that they asked me what my profession was before the war. I had other professions and occupations, but I don't want to mention them again. After the war started and after I was wounded, I was transferred into the civilian structures, where I was in charge of collecting humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did somebody appointed you to the duty of collecting humanitarian aid? Did you receive an order or an authority to do that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Probably somebody appointed me, but I wouldn't be able to say who it was now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain to the Trial Chamber how humanitarian aid was collected in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I'm saying how we could work in the territory of my branch office. We sowed wheat. We [indiscernible] plums, and we would distribute to the people what we had. And when a convoy arrived we would also distribute flour or whatever arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was humanitarian aid sold in Srebrenica over the counter?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know that there were such instances. It -- this may have happened, but I had nothing to do with the influx of aid into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who was entitled to humanitarian aid by social class?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know what the priorities were, but I know that a kilo or at the most a kilo and a half per head of the family were distributed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I stopped you. You should wait for the end of the answer. Now put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As the representative of your region, did you receive information about the arrival of aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No. Nobody could know when the Serb soldiers would let a convoy pass at Bratunac or Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was there a warehouse of any sort in Srebrenica where the humanitarian aid was kept until the representatives of the local communes or the villages arrived to distribute it?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Probably there was a warehouse for flour and oil and the like, but I had nothing to do with that. There was another man who transported it. We only distributed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that the aid for your village or region could not be distributed without you knowing about that?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We made decisions collectively. It wasn't myself who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were drawing, or rather, marking in the photograph the classrooms in which you were, 1, 2, and 3, you said for the transcript that there were about 200 prisoners in the classroom where you were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. I say that the classroom was big enough for about 200 people. I cannot say with any certainty whether there were 190 or 210, but around 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You also said that there were three classrooms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that there were three classrooms on the upper floor that I was able to see, or rather, which I was able to observe in running past. But I believe that on the storey beneath there may also have been classrooms and there may have been other classrooms on the upper floor too. I'm pretty sure there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, that's easy to establish. So if we suppose that on the ground floor there were as many classrooms as on the upper floor, which seems logical, does it mean that every classroom was big enough for about 200 people?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If there was six classrooms, that adds up to 1200 people?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: But I can repeat, I don't know how many classrooms there were. I suppose that the gymnasium was also used or people may have been brought there earlier. I didn't have time and I was too scared to count the classrooms, but I know that I saw three and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How large is -- was that classroom?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Well, some question this is. I was in no position to measure the classroom. I wasn't sure whether I would survive, let alone to think of measuring the classroom. It would have been 40 square metres large or 50 at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were there also Serb soldiers in that classroom; and if so, where did they stand?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, they would come in all the time and control us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was the area next to the door reserved for Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Your Honours, I apologise. Can anything be seen on our screens? Are there our images or am I mistaken? I must have been mistaken. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. You were asked, were Serb soldiers in that classroom? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. The Serb soldiers didn't stay in the classroom with us, but they were standing guard at the door and they would come in often demanding money, gold, jewellery. If we had any of those, we had to collect them. They would give us 15 to 20 minutes to do so. Occasionally they would butt in, two or three of them. And around the building and in front of us there were Serb soldiers all the time and we would hear bursts of fire often, and the Serb soldiers were standing in the hallway. I hope I made myself clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That was quite clear. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you said that you were brought to Kravica on trucks; correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What model of truck was that? Would you be able to recognise it if you were shown a picture?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can't recognise them, but I believe they were military trucks. I think I can tell by the tarpaulins.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were those the regular military trucks with benches or were they of the kind that you saw when you were a soldier?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: There were no benches. Whether there had been any previously, I don't know, but they had tight tarpaulins. And -- but the back side wasn't closed with the tarpaulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it a TAM truck? Were they TAM trucks?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can repeat once more that we were frightened to death and we didn't dare raise our heads. I believe they were military trucks, but whether they were TAMs or any other make, I can't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber the size of the trucks roughly, how long and how wide they were?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Well, if a hundred people would fit into it and some of them were even larger, for 200 people, and they may have been 7 to 8 metres long and 3 metres wide, but I don't know much of -- about trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that 119 people were on your truck, that they were counted; right?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, we were counted while we were still at Kravica, while we were still focused enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you sit on those trucks?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes. I sat on the floor and a man was sitting on my lap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you will have realised that your next question was not recorded because I stopped you. You were again overlapping, and this is not appropriate. We want to have a good translation and a good transcript. If you continue in that way, that will cause many problems. We have to break now, the second break for today, and you should focus on the time, Mr. Tolimir, so that we will be able to finish the -- with this witness and your cross-examination quite soon. We adjourn and we resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Tolimir, I would like to raise one confusion which occurred in the transcript on page 65, line 20. There is mentioned a document 2D50. In fact it should be page 2.950 of the transcript of the previous trial. The same occurred in -- on page 66, line 14, instead of 2D52, it should be 2.952. That is only just for the sake of the transcript. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: To keep up the continuity of what we were talking about before the break, could we please show the witness the statement that he gave to the OTP. The reference is D --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D82, page 5 of the Serbian version, the last-but-one paragraph; and page 5 in the English version, the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will not be broadcasted outside of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 5 of the Serbian version we see the last paragraph, which I would like to read out: "They started to put us on trucks and we were driven toward Kravica. I again saw five or six trucks. The men on my truck counted 119 of us. When we reached Konjevic Polje, I saw that we were turning toward Kravica. We arrived in the evening, around 1700 or 1730 hours, on the 13th of July. The Serbs told us we were in Kravica. I knew Kravica well. My truck parked on the road in front of a supermarket. Two trucks parked behind the truck on which I was and one or two in front. The Serbs asked who was taking part in the take-over of Kravica when it fell under BiH control." End of quote from page 5 of the witness's statement to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here's my question: Were all these trucks the same model as the one on which you were?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that the two that I was able to see behind mine were the same; and the others that I saw, the two or three, at Nova Kasaba, I'm not sure. But these two were the same and they came to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So there were five trucks in all in Kravica, right, two behind yours and two in front of yours?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I can repeat that I was able to see two behind mine, and the other two I saw when we were put on the trucks at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me repeat to you the last sentence from that paragraph: "Two trucks parked behind my truck and one or two in front of it." Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: It is correct that there were two trucks behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And is it also correct that two were in front?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I cannot state that with certainty, but we heard screams at night when they were taking people away and killing them and slaughtering them. So I suppose that there must have been other trucks in front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you didn't pause again, and let me tell you your quotation was not correct. In the statement it is said one or two parked in front. Your quotation was different. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like the witness to say whether at Kravica he saw five trucks, as we see in this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally saw three trucks, and there may have been others further ahead, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you able to see trucks when you got off them from Kravica to the place of the execution?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to see them -- I was able to see trucks in Zvornik, in front of the school, three trucks. Whether there were more, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If there were three trucks, could 2.000 or 3.000 people fit in three trucks?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Let me repeat. I wasn't able to count the trucks nor what was on them. I gave an estimate of the number of dead bodies at the execution site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please explain to the Trial Chamber the basis for your estimate, how you -- how did you arrive at your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Based on the size of the plateau and how many people could fit on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you determine the number of people based on the number of trucks that had arrived? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Of course, I'm sure that it was possible if you knew how many people were brought to the school during the day, but we don't know how many people were brought and how many trucks arrived at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you about the part that you saw yourself. Did you see only three trucks and not more? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I repeat, I saw only three trucks while I was jumping down from my lorry. Let me tell you what state I was in. I'd been in the lorry for 24 hours, my leg hurt, somebody was sitting in my lap, I was at a gunpoint all that time. If you had been in my position, would you be able to count the trucks? I saw three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I just wanted to hear what you saw and what you heard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the session be closed, please. Can we go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, yes, private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank the witness for the answers provided during his testimony. I would like to thank the OTP for bringing him here. I would like to thank you, and I would like to apologise to the interpreters for overlapping and making their jobs difficult in producing a clear and unambiguous transcript. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir. I hope very much that this will be a lesson in slowing down for the sake of the interpreters. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has some questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: If I refer you back to your testimony of this morning, somewhere you state that you were cut off from the column. Can you just explain how you were cut off from the column.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Well, it was very simple. When the Serb forces ambushed us at Kamenicko Brdo, as it is known, that was a major ambush, we were broken up into small groups. My relative, or my cousin, was wounded on that occasion and I tried to save his life. And that's why we got separated from the main body of the column, and we remained in that little brook. In the morning we didn't know what to do and where to go. During the night it was very foggy, we were not familiar with the terrain, and since we had seen a lot of dead bodies up there including my brother -- actually, my brother went missing during that ambush, we simply got lost. We were afraid. We got cut off from the column, and by morning, by the dawn, we had a few wounded and we didn't know where we were and in which direction to take after that brook, after that little thicket. And the Serb shelling started immediately after that. And all that time we could -- were able to observe a white UN APC which was moving from Kravica towards Konjevic Polje and vice versa. And we could hear a voice from the APC calling out to us to surrender, that our safety was guaranteed, that we should not get killed, that we should save our wounded, that we would be exchanged, that they would guarantee our safety, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your explanation. Just another follow-up question. You also testified that there were grenades thrown at the column. Can you just clarify who threw the column [sic] because you also testified that there were some among your column who had grenades. These grenades, were they thrown by people outside the column or people within the column or both?

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. There may have been a few people who had hand-grenades and maybe they had thrown them. In any case, we were shelled all that time from Serb positions. They used PATs and PAMs and they fired shells on our lines from the forest. As the crow flies that was about 200 or 300 metres away from the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. On the left side of the forest through which we were moving, there were a lot of people wounded by the Serbian shelling, by the fire opened from PATs, PAMs, and by the hand-grenades that the Serb soldiers had thrown at the column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one last question for you. You also stated that when you survived, you survived with one other person, a man younger than you. Do you know what happened to this person? Did you meet up anywhere or did you lose each other somewhere? Can you just clarify for me.

utterances.speaker: PW-015
utterances.text: Yes, that was a younger person. He was a minor who was maybe 15 or 16 at the time. He was even more seriously wounded than me. In that ditch I took off my T-shirt, I dressed his wounds, and together we pulled out of that ditch. And we walked together through the woods all the time and we crossed over to the free territory on the same day. I still maintain contact with that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Does any party have follow-up question after these answers? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, no, I have no follow-up questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, do you have any additional question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Trial Chamber please ask the witness whether he knows if that person provided a statement to either the BiH organs or the OTP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know -- I believe that he did provide a statement to the OTP and that he has testified here at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, the Chamber and all present in the courtroom would like to thank you that you were able to come to The Hague again and to assist the Chamber to establish the truth and what happened. Thank you very much again, and you are free now to return to your normal activities, and we wish you all the best for your future life. Thank you again --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- and we go into private session so that you may leave the courtroom without any -- without being recorded outside. Closed session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, thank you for your patience, but we had to wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for your indulgence, Mr. President. I just wanted to -- for the Court's convenience to indicate for the record that the witness -- that the present witness indicated he'd given a prior statement. It is Witness PW-008, it's a 92 bis witness and the statement number is 65 ter number 41, just for the Court's reference and for the Court's convenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That is very helpful. What is the situation and the position of the Prosecution? Is there a next witness? We have exactly 16 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The witness number -- I'm sorry, Mr. President. The Witness number is 41. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer, I can't see you very well behind the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Investigator Blaszczyk is available and we can get some work done in the remaining 15 minutes if the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness be brought in, please, just to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation which is shown to you on the card now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. We have only a quarter of an hour left in our today's hearings, but we should start with your examination. Mr. Thayer has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state and spell your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: My name is Tomasz Blaszczyk, B-l-a-s-z-c-z-y-k.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it's no secret and I take it from all the consonants that you're a native of Poland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, I am from Poland.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you currently work as an investigator for the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How long have you been an investigator with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I have been working for OTP since 2003, January.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you give the Trial Chamber just a brief idea of which investigations you've had occasion to work on.

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Most of the time since I arrived to the ICTY, I've been appointed to the investigation regarding the Srebrenica events. And only few months, in 2005, I've been deployed to one of the Kosovo cases. And later on, in 2006, I returned to Srebrenica investigation team.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what kind of work, again briefly, did you do before you came to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Before I came to the OTP, I joined the OTP, I was a police officer back in home, in Poland.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And what kind of police work did you do there?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: At the beginning I was uniformed police officer, and then I joined criminal investigation unit in my region, region of Gdansk in Poland.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in connection with your police work, did you ever have occasion to work or travel to the area we now refer to as the former Yugoslavia or Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes. During my work with the Polish police, I was deployed three times to Bosnia as international police officer and also one time in Croatia or -- this is former Krajina or so-called Krajina in Croatia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just for the record, you made your debut as the official gap-filler back in the Popovic case and you testified here and there over a period of four days about the topic that you're here today to testify about, that is, the Drina Corps collection; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just let me put the dates on the record. It may come up later. Those dates were 2 November, 22 November, 28 November, and 4 December 2007. And in the Popovic case did you also testify on another topic, that is, the -- what we refer to as the Petrovic video that was taken by a journalist by the name of Zoran Petrovic, Pirocanac?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. I testified about this Petrovic video in so-called road book regarding Petrovic video.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And this road book that you just referred to is essentially a map-sized book that's designed to assist the Trial Chamber in providing some more detail for the video; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: That's correct, except the maps we had -- we have in this book also some pictures from the various places around Srebrenica, Bratunac, Sandici, and Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And again just so the record is clear, you're going to come back and testify in this case about that road book as well at a future date; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's talk about this Drina Corps collection of documents, as we've referred to it. When did you yourself first learn that this collection of documents had been located?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: First time I heard of this collection had been located, it was sometime in the middle of December 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And who first told you about it?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who first told me that, but definitely had to be my team leader or one person from the management.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And to your knowledge, sir, who in the OTP first became aware that this large volume of documents had been located?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: As far as I know, the first was informed our management chief of investigation at that time in OTP, I believe, and our -- possible that also our field office investigator in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And who is that person, sir, and where does that person work in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: It was Finn Tollefsen, our investigator, former investigator. He doesn't work anymore for OTP, as he was at that time deployed to our field office in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber, as a result of your personal involvement and subsequent investigation that was conducted, can you describe for the Trial Chamber just how this collection came to be located and then how it came to be in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: I got this information from management later on, from my own review of the papers we received. As far as I know, the collection was located by minister of interior or minister of defence of Republika Srpska. The collection was found in Serbia, in the place called Gornji Milanovac, and then it was agreed with Serbian authorities that the collection would be collected by the commission appointed by Republika Srpska authority and taken back to Bosnia. And it happened, it happened on the night of December 2004. Joint commission -- commission, in fact, members of MOD and Ministry of the Interior went to Gornji Milanovac to collect this so-called collection, Drina Corps collection. The collection first was taken to Banja Luka and located at the premises of Ministry of Interior. The key from the padlocks of this collection, because the paper -- the collection was located in 16 cases, boxes, was kept by the members of Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. And later on, on the 13th of December, 2004, meeting was -- took place in our office, field office, in Banja Luka, where it was decided that collection -- that these 15 -- these 16 boxes will be kept at our premises, I mean premises of ICTY, in Banja Luka. And after that it was agreed that the boxes will be -- the contents of the boxes will be taken to The Hague. And in next few days, in -- it was on the 15th and 16th, the boxes were checked by SFOR, or at the time I think it was EUFOR team, for possible explosive materiel. And after that, the boxes -- the contents of the boxes were repacked to another boxes. And on the 17th of December, 2004, the new boxes were taken to our field office in Zagreb. And at the time on 17th of December, 2004, I was present in Zagreb. The same day, before the boxes arrived to Zagreb, our Zagreb field office, I also arrived to our Zagreb field office. And after initial reviewing of the contents of the boxes, we described to re-pack these boxes again, the contents of these boxes again to another boxes, to 55 boxes. And I made, as I said, I made initial assessment of the content of the boxes. We realised that this is collection of Drina Corps. And after -- after that, the boxes, on the 3rd [Realtime transcript read in error "5th"] of January, 2005, were transported to The Hague and came to The Hague on the 4th of January, 2005, and contents was located in our evidence unit here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And once the documents made it into the evidence unit of the OTP, what happened with them then?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: We organised this collection, the entire documentation, in such way that would be available for everybody in the Tribunal, for each case, for each team, for everybody, in fact. We reviewed the documents again. It was team who did it. And we organised this documentation in this way, that first we divided the entire collection for -- let's say for the units, like Drina Corps, like units subordinated to Drina Corps, like -- like Zvornik Brigade, Bratunac Brigade, Sekovici Brigade, after that by the branch, it means that, for example, the logistic documents, operational documents, security branch documents, and after that, in sequence by date. And of course, after that, the collection was MIF'd by us. It means that we created -- our team created kind of information form for each batch of the documents. And after that, the documents were stamped by people from the evidence unit and put in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify one thing, sir. On our LiveNote at page 94, line 19, it indicates that you testified that the boxes were transported on the 5th of January to The Hague and that they arrived on the 4th of January. Could you just clarify the dates, please, for us so we know exactly what date they left Zagreb and what date they arrived in The Hague, please?

utterances.speaker: TOMASZ BLASZCZYK
utterances.text: The boxes left Zagreb on the 3rd of January, 3 January, 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do next, sir, is back up and ask you some questions about the background to these documents as you learned about it through your investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that would probably be better to pick up tomorrow morning, if we could, Mr. President, since that's a new chapter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Thayer. That concludes the examination, the first part of your examination for today. We have to adjourn. Please be informed that you may not discuss with anybody of either party about the content of your testimony here in the trial --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- during the break. We adjourn now and resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of April, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
